arXiv:2203.14403v1 [math.AP] 27 Mar 2022

Improvement on the blow-up for a weakly coupled wave equations with scale-invariant damping and mass and time derivative nonlinearity

Makram Hamouda1 and Mohamed Ali Hamza1 Address: 1 Department of Basic Sciences, Deanship of Preparatory Year and Supporting Studies, Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University, P. O. Box 1982, Dammam, Saudi Arabia. Email address: mmhamouda@iau.edu.sa (M. Hamouda) Email address: mahamza@iau.edu.sa (M.A. Hamza)
Abstract.

An improvement of [18] on the blow-up region and the lifespan estimate of a weakly coupled system of wave equations with damping and mass in the scale-invariant case and with time-derivative nonlinearity is obtained in this article. Indeed, thanks to a better understanding of the dynamics of the solutions, we give here a better characterization of the blow-up region. Furthermore, the techniques used in this article may be extended to other systems and interestingly they simplify the proof of the blow-up result in [3] which is concerned with the single wave equation in the same context as in the present work.

Key words and phrases: 
blow-up, critical curve, lifespan, nonlinear wave equations, semilinear weakly coupled system, scale-invariant damping, time-derivative nonlinearity.
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
35L71, 35B44

1. Introduction

The weakly coupled system of semilinear wave equations in the presence of damping and mass terms in scale-invariant case with time derivative nonlinearity reads as follows:

(1.1) {ut​t−Δ​u+μ11+t​ut+ν12(1+t)2​u=|∂tv|p,(x,t)∈ℝN×[0,∞),vt​t−Δ​v+μ21+t​vt+ν22(1+t)2​v=|∂tu|q,(x,t)∈ℝN×[0,∞),u(x,0)=εf1(x),v(x,0)=εf2(x),x∈ℝN,ut(x,0)=εg1(x),vt(x,0)=εg2(x),x∈ℝN,\displaystyle\begin{cases}\displaystyle u_{tt}-\Delta u+\frac{\mu_{1}}{1+t}u_{t}+\frac{\nu_{1}^{2}}{(1+t)^{2}}u=|\partial_{t}v|^{p},&\quad(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),\\ \displaystyle v_{tt}-\Delta v+\frac{\mu_{2}}{1+t}v_{t}+\frac{\nu_{2}^{2}}{(1+t)^{2}}v=|\partial_{t}u|^{q},&\quad(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),\\ u(x,0)={\varepsilon}f_{1}(x),\ \ v(x,0)={\varepsilon}f_{2}(x),&\quad x\in\mathbb{R}^{N},\\ u_{t}(x,0)={\varepsilon}g_{1}(x),\ \ v_{t}(x,0)=\varepsilon g_{2}(x),&\quad x\in\mathbb{R}^{N},\end{cases}

where μ1,μ2,ν12\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\nu^{2}_{1} and ν22\nu^{2}_{2} are nonnegative constants. The positive parameter ε{\varepsilon} characterizes the size of the initial data, and f1,f2,g1f_{1},f_{2},g_{1} and g2g_{2} are positive functions assumed to be compactly supported on BℝN​(0,R),R>0B_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}(0,R),R>0.
Naturally, along this article , we suppose that p,q>1p,q>1.

First, we recall the Glassey exponent pGp_{G} which is given by

(1.2) pG=pG​(N):=1+2N−1.p_{G}=p_{G}(N):=1+\frac{2}{N-1}.

It is well-known that the aforementioned critical value, pGp_{G}, characterizes the threshold between the global existence (p>pGp>p_{G}) and the nonexistence (p≤pGp\leq p_{G}) regions; see e.g. [7, 8, 10, 20, 23, 26].

In this paragraph, we recall some results related the massless case for a single equation. We start by mentioning the blow-up result for the solution of a single equation inherited from (1.1) without mass term. Indeed, Lai and Takamura showed in [13] an upper bound estimate of the lifespan. Later, in [18], Palmieri and Tu enhanced this result by extending the blow-up region for pp in the case of a single equation (with mass term). More precisely, they obtain a blow-up result for p∈(1,pG​(N+σ⁡(μ,0))]p\in(1,p_{G}(N+\sigma(\mu,0))] where

(1.3) σ=σ⁡(μ,ν):={μ+1−δifδ∈[0,1),μifδ≥1,\sigma=\sigma(\mu,\nu):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\mu+1-\sqrt{\delta}&\textnormal{if}&\delta\in[0,1),\\ \mu&\text{if}&\delta\geq 1,\end{array}\right.

and δ\delta is given by (1.5) below. Note that the result in [18] was recently improved in [6] by extending the upper bound for pp from pG​(N+σ⁡(μ,0))p_{G}(N+\sigma(\mu,0)) to pG​(N+μ)p_{G}(N+\mu).

Recently, in [3], the case of the scale-invariant damped equation with mass and time-derivative nonlinearity was studied; this reads

(1.4) {ut​t−Δ​u+μ1+t​ut+ν2(1+t)2​u=|ut|p,in​ℝN×[0,∞),u(x,0)=εf(x),ut(x,0)=εg(x),x∈ℝN.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle u_{tt}-\Delta u+\frac{\mu}{1+t}u_{t}+\frac{\nu^{2}}{(1+t)^{2}}u=|u_{t}|^{p},\quad\mbox{in}\ {\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),\\ u(x,0)={\varepsilon}f(x),\ u_{t}(x,0)={\varepsilon}g(x),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}.\end{array}\right.

Let us introduce the following quantity, that we assume to be positive,

(1.5) δ=δ⁡(μ,ν):=(μ−1)2−4​ν2.\delta=\delta(\mu,\nu):=(\mu-1)^{2}-4\nu^{2}.

Furthermore, we define

(1.6) σ=σ⁡(μ,ν):={μ+1−δifδ∈[0,1),μifδ≥1.\sigma=\sigma(\mu,\nu):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\mu+1-\sqrt{\delta}&\textnormal{if}&\delta\in[0,1),\\ \mu&\text{if}&\delta\geq 1.\end{array}\right.

Using a functional approach, a blow-up result is proven in [3] for (1.4), improving thus the one obtained in [18]. In fact, the blow-up interval, p∈(1,pG​(N+σ)]p\in(1,p_{G}(N+\sigma)] (σ\sigma is given by (1.6)), is ameliorated in comparison with [18], to show the blow-up inside the region p∈(1,pG​(N+μ)]p\in(1,p_{G}(N+\mu)], with δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). However, for δ≥1\delta\geq 1, the two results, in [3] and [18], are the same. In relationship with these works, we also mention the articles [6, 13] where the massless case is investigated.

Now, letting μ1=μ2=ν1=ν2=0\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\nu_{1}=\nu_{2}=0 in (1.1) we find the following coupled system:

(1.7) {ut​t−Δ​u=|∂tv|p,(x,t)∈ℝN×[0,∞),vt​t−Δ​v=|∂tu|q,(x,t)∈ℝN×[0,∞),u(x,0)=εf1(x),v(x,0)=εf2(x),x∈ℝN,ut(x,0)=εg1(x),vt(x,0)=εg2(x),x∈ℝN.\displaystyle\begin{cases}u_{tt}-\Delta u=|\partial_{t}v|^{p},&(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),\\ v_{tt}-\Delta v=|\partial_{t}u|^{q},&(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),\\ u(x,0)={\varepsilon}f_{1}(x),\ \ v(x,0)={\varepsilon}f_{2}(x),&x\in\mathbb{R}^{N},\\ u_{t}(x,0)={\varepsilon}g_{1}(x),\ \ v_{t}(x,0)=\varepsilon g_{2}(x),&x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}.\end{cases}

For the global existence of solutions to (1.7), we refer the reader to [11]. However, the blow-up of (1.7) has been the subject of several works; see e.g. [1, 9, 15, 16]. More precisely, the critical (in the sense of interface between blow-up and global existence) curve for p,qp,q is given by

(1.8) Υ⁡(N,p,q):=max⁡(Λ⁡(N,p,q),Λ⁡(N,q,p))=0,\Upsilon(N,p,q):=\max(\Lambda(N,p,q),\Lambda(N,q,p))=0,

where

(1.9) Λ⁡(N,p,q):=p+1p​q−1−N−12.\displaystyle\Lambda(N,p,q):=\frac{p+1}{pq-1}-\frac{N-1}{2}.

Under some assumptions, the solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.7) blows up in finite time T⁡(ε)T({\varepsilon}) for small initial data (of size ε{\varepsilon}), namely

(1.10) T⁡(ε)≤{C​ε−Υ⁡(N,p,q)ifΥ⁡(N,p,q)>0,exp⁡(C​ε−(p​q−1))ifΥ(N,p,q)=0,p≠q,exp⁡(C​ε−(p−1))ifΥ(N,p,q)=0,p=q.T({\varepsilon})\leq\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}C{\varepsilon}^{-\Upsilon(N,p,q)}&\text{if}&\Upsilon(N,p,q)>0,\\ \exp(C{\varepsilon}^{-(pq-1)})&\text{if}&\Upsilon(N,p,q)=0,\ p\neq q,\\ \exp(C{\varepsilon}^{-(p-1)})&\text{if}&\Upsilon(N,p,q)=0,\ p=q.\end{array}\right.

In the context of the present work, Palmieri and Tu [18] proved a blow-up result for the system (1.1). More precisely, the authors in [18] proved that there is blow-up for the system (1.1) for p,qp,q satisfying

(1.11) Ω⁡(N,σ1,σ2,p,q):=max⁡(Λ⁡(N+σ1,p,q),Λ⁡(N+σ2,q,p))≥0,\Omega(N,\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},p,q):=\max(\Lambda(N+\sigma_{1},p,q),\Lambda(N+\sigma_{2},q,p))\geq 0,

where Λ\Lambda is given by (1.9) and σi=σ(μi,νi),i=1,2\sigma_{i}=\sigma(\mu_{i},\nu_{i}),i=1,2 is given by (1.6).
Indeed, for small initial data (of size ε{\varepsilon}), the solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.1) blows up in finite time T⁡(ε)T({\varepsilon}) that is bounded as

(1.12) T⁡(ε)≤{C​ε−Ω⁡(N,σ1,σ2,p,q)ifΩ⁡(N,σ1,σ2,p,q)>0,exp⁡(C​ε−(p​q−1))ifΩ⁡(N,σ1,σ2,p,q)=0,exp⁡(C​ε−min⁡(p​q−1p+1,p​q−1q+1))ifΛ⁡(N+σ1,p,q)=Λ⁡(N+σ2,p,q)=0.T({\varepsilon})\leq\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}C{\varepsilon}^{-\Omega(N,\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},p,q)}&\text{if}&\Omega(N,\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},p,q)>0,\\ \exp(C{\varepsilon}^{-(pq-1)})&\text{if}&\Omega(N,\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},p,q)=0,\\ \exp(C{\varepsilon}^{-\min\left(\frac{pq-1}{p+1},\frac{pq-1}{q+1}\right)})&\text{if}&\Lambda(N+\sigma_{1},p,q)=\Lambda(N+\sigma_{2},p,q)=0.\end{array}\right.

Concerning the case of coupled equations, namely (1.1) without mass terms (ν1=ν2=0\nu_{1}=\nu_{2}=0), an improvement was obtained in [5] for the blow-up results and the lifespan. The results in [5] are ameliorating the ones in [18].

In this article, we refine the results in [18] when at least one of the coefficients δi,i=1,2\delta_{i},i=1,2, is in [0,1)[0,1). In fact, for positive values of δi\delta_{i} (i=1,2i=1,2), we extend the results obtained in [18] to show that the new blow-up region does not depend on the mass parameters νi,i=1,2\nu_{i},i=1,2 (and hence nor on σi,i=1,2\sigma_{i},i=1,2). A similar observation was concluded for the case of a one equation that we studied in [3], and the aim here is to extend this examination to the case of the coupled system (1.1). But, although the obtaining of similar results for damped coupled systems with mass terms is predictable, the situation is somehow more delicate. Indeed, the techniques used in [3] are now longer effective for the system (1.1). To overcome this difficulty, we first write the linear problem associated with (1.1) which reduces in this case to the following single equation:

(1.13) wt​tL−Δ​wL+μi1+t​wtL+νi2(1+t)2​wL=0,\displaystyle\displaystyle w^{L}_{tt}-\Delta w^{L}+\frac{\mu_{i}}{1+t}w^{L}_{t}+\frac{\nu_{i}^{2}}{(1+t)^{2}}w^{L}=0,

where ww stands for uLu^{L} or vLv^{L}, the solutions of the linear problem associated with (1.1).
Clearly, the equation (1.13) is invariant under the following transformation:

(1.14) w~L​(x,t)=wL​(α​x,α⁡(1+t)−1),α>0.\displaystyle\tilde{w}^{L}(x,t)=w^{L}(\alpha x,\alpha(1+t)-1),\ \alpha>0.

Taking advantage of the aforementioned invariance properties, we refine our choice for a functional family that is indexed by a positive parameter η\eta. This judicious choice implies a better description of the dynamics of the solution of (1.1). More precisely, we obtain, for η\eta large enough, the coercivity of the functional that will be introduced later on to show the blow-up results.

Thanks to the above observations, we finally enhance the result on the blow-up region, defined by (1.11) and obtained in [18], by showing that the critical curve is characterized by

(1.15) Ω⁡(N,μ1,μ2,p,q)=max⁡(Λ⁡(N+μ1,p,q),Λ⁡(N+μ2,q,p))≥0,\Omega(N,\mu_{1},\mu_{2},p,q)=\max(\Lambda(N+\mu_{1},p,q),\Lambda(N+\mu_{2},q,p))\geq 0,

where Λ\Lambda is given by (1.9).

The outline of this article is presented as follows. First, we introduce in Section 2 the weak formulation of (1.1) in the energy space. Then, in the same section, we state our main result. Some technical lemmas are proven in Section 3. Finally, we show the proof of the main result in Section 4.

2. Main Result

The aim of this section is to state our main result for which we will write the equivalent of the system (1.1) in the corresponding energy space. More precisely, the weak formulation associated with (1.1) reads as follows:

Definition 2.1.

We say that (u,v)(u,v) is an energy solution of (1.1) on [0,T)[0,T) if

{u,v∈𝒞⁡([0,T),H1​(ℝN))∩𝒞1​([0,T),L2​(ℝN)),ut∈Ll​o​cq​((0,T)×ℝN),vt∈Ll​o​cp​((0,T)×ℝN)\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u,v\in\mathcal{C}([0,T),H^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}))\cap\mathcal{C}^{1}([0,T),L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})),\\ \ u_{t}\in L^{q}_{loc}((0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N}),\ v_{t}\in L^{p}_{loc}((0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N})\end{array}\right.

satisfies, for all Φ,Φ~∈𝒞0∞​(ℝN×[0,T))\Phi,\tilde{\Phi}\in\mathcal{C}_{0}^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,T)) and all t∈[0,T)t\in[0,T), the following equations:

together with the conditions u⁡(x,0)=ε​f1​(x)u(x,0)=\varepsilon f_{1}(x) and v⁡(x,0)=ε​f2​(x)v(x,0)=\varepsilon f_{2}(x) being satisfied in H1​(ℝN)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{N}).
After some elementary computations, (2.1) and (2.2) can be written, respectively, in the following way

(2.3) ∫ℝN[ut​(x,t)​Φ​(x,t)−u⁡(x,t)​Φt​(x,t)+μ11+t​u​(x,t)​Φ​(x,t)]​𝑑x∫0t∫ℝNu⁡(x,s)​[Φt​t​(x,s)−Δ​Φ​(x,s)−∂∂s​(μ1+s​Φ​(x,s))+ν12(1+s)2​Φ​(x,s)]​𝑑x​𝑑s=∫0t∫ℝN|ut​(x,s)|p​Φ​(x,s)​dx​ds+ε​∫ℝN[−f1​(x)​Φt​(x,0)+(μ1​f1​(x)+g1​(x))​Φ​(x,0)]​dx,\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\big[u_{t}(x,t)\Phi(x,t)-u(x,t)\Phi_{t}(x,t)+\frac{\mu_{1}}{1+t}u(x,t)\Phi(x,t)\big]dx\\ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}u(x,s)\left[\Phi_{tt}(x,s)-\Delta\Phi(x,s)-\frac{\partial}{\partial s}\left(\frac{\mu}{1+s}\Phi(x,s)\right)+\frac{\nu_{1}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}\Phi(x,s)\right]dx\,ds\\ \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}|u_{t}(x,s)|^{p}\Phi(x,s)dx\,ds+{\varepsilon}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\big[-f_{1}(x)\Phi_{t}(x,0)+\left(\mu_{1}f_{1}(x)+g_{1}(x)\right)\Phi(x,0)\big]dx,\end{array}

and

Remark 2.1.

Since ff and gg are supported on BℝN​(0,R)B_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}(0,R), one can see that supp​(u),supp​(v)⊂{(x,t)∈ℝN×[0,∞):|x|≤t+R}\mbox{\rm supp}(u),\mbox{\rm supp}(v)\ \subset\{(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty):|x|\leq t+R\}. Consequently, one can choose any test function Φ\Phi which is not necessarily compactly supported.

In the following, we state the main result of this article.

Let p,q>1p,q>1. For i=1,2i=1,2, let μi,νi2>0\mu_{i},\nu_{i}^{2}>0, with δi:=δ⁡(μi,νi)>0\delta_{i}:=\delta(\mu_{i},\nu_{i})>0 (see (1.5)), such that

(2.5) Ω⁡(N,μ1,μ2,p,q)≥0,\Omega(N,\mu_{1},\mu_{2},p,q)\geq 0,

(2.6) μi−1−δi2fi(x)+gi(x)≥0,i=1,2.\frac{\mu_{i}-1-\sqrt{\delta_{i}}}{2}f_{i}(x)+g_{i}(x)\geq 0,\quad i=1,2.

(2.7) T⁡(ε)≤{C​ε−Ω⁡(N,μ1,μ2,p,q)ifΩ⁡(N,μ1,μ2,p,q)>0,exp⁡(C​ε−(p​q−1))ifΩ⁡(N,μ1,μ2,p,q)=0,exp⁡(C​ε−min⁡(p​q−1p+1,p​q−1q+1))ifΛ⁡(N+μ1,p,q)=Λ⁡(N+μ2,q,p)=0.T({\varepsilon})\leq\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}C{\varepsilon}^{-\Omega(N,\mu_{1},\mu_{2},p,q)}&\text{if}&\Omega(N,\mu_{1},\mu_{2},p,q)>0,\\ \exp(C{\varepsilon}^{-(pq-1)})&\text{if}&\Omega(N,\mu_{1},\mu_{2},p,q)=0,\\ \exp(C{\varepsilon}^{-\min\left(\frac{pq-1}{p+1},\frac{pq-1}{q+1}\right)})&\text{if}&\Lambda(N+\mu_{1},p,q)=\Lambda(N+\mu_{2},q,p)=0.\end{array}\right.

where CC is a positive constant independent of ε{\varepsilon} and 0<ε≤ε00<{\varepsilon}\leq{\varepsilon}_{0}.

Remark 2.2.

The blow-up result in Theorem 2.2 exhibits the new region obtained for the critical curve for p,qp,q as a shift of the dimension by μ1,μ2\mu_{1},\mu_{2}. We believe that this new blow-up region delimitation coincides with the critical one. Of course, a rigorous confirmation should be proved by a global existence result.

Remark 2.3.

The result in Theorem 2.2 holds true for the following generalized system:

(2.8) {ut​t−Δ​u+(b1​(t)+μ11+t)​ut+(c1​(t)+ν12(1+t)2)​u=|∂tv|p,(x,t)∈ℝN×[0,∞),vt​t−Δ​v+(b2​(t)+μ21+t)​vt+(c2​(t)+ν22(1+t)2)​v=|∂tu|q,(x,t)∈ℝN×[0,∞),\displaystyle\begin{cases}\displaystyle u_{tt}-\Delta u+\left(b_{1}(t)+\frac{\mu_{1}}{1+t}\right)u_{t}+\left(c_{1}(t)+\frac{\nu_{1}^{2}}{(1+t)^{2}}\right)u=|\partial_{t}v|^{p},&\ (x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),\\ \displaystyle v_{tt}-\Delta v+\left(b_{2}(t)+\frac{\mu_{2}}{1+t}\right)v_{t}+\left(c_{2}(t)+\frac{\nu_{2}^{2}}{(1+t)^{2}}\right)v=|\partial_{t}u|^{q},&\ (x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),\end{cases}

where bi​(t),(1+t)​ci​(t)b_{i}(t),(1+t)c_{i}(t) belong to L1​(0,∞)L^{1}(0,\infty) and μi,νi\mu_{i},\nu_{i} are such that δi>0\delta_{i}>0; i=1,2i=1,2.
The proof of the generalized damping case (2.8) can be performed by mimicking the one of Theorem 2.2 with the necessary modifications.

Remark 2.4.

The techniques used in this article can be of course adapted in other contexts. More precisely, the case of a single equation corresponding to (1.1) can be simplified by taking into account the invariance property (1.14) which is related to the introduction of the parameter η\eta. Furthermore, one can use the aforementioned techniques to study systems like (1.1) with mixed nonlinearities, this will be the subject of a forthcoming work which will somehow constitute an extension of our previous works [4, 5, 6], see also [13, 17].

3. Some auxiliary results

We first introduce a positive test function which is defined as

(3.1) ψiη(x,t):=ρiη(t)ϕη(x),i=1,2,∀η>0,\psi_{i}^{\eta}(x,t):=\rho_{i}^{\eta}(t)\phi^{\eta}(x),\ i=1,2,\ \forall\ \eta>0,

Note that the function ϕη​(x)\phi^{\eta}(x) is introduced in [25] and ρiη​(t)\rho_{i}^{\eta}(t), [15, 19, 21, 22], is solution of

Remark 3.1.

One can note that the lower bounds in Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 are not optimal. However, the aforementioned results are sufficient to prove our main result since we only need the positivity of Fiη​(t)F_{i}^{\eta}(t) and F~iη​(t),i=1,2\tilde{F}_{i}^{\eta}(t),\ i=1,2, for all t>1t>1. To enhance these lower bounds, we will instead introduce new functionals as we will see in the next lemmas.

Although the computations in the rest of this article can be carried out for all η≥η0\eta\geq\eta_{0}, we choose from now to set η=η0\eta=\eta_{0} and ignore the dependence on η\eta for all the functions (already introduced or which will be later on) that will be subsequently used. For example, the function ψiη\psi_{i}^{\eta} will be simply denoted by ψi\psi_{i}, and the same for all the other functions (including the constants) unless otherwise specified.

The following functionals can be now introduced and will be used subsequently in the proof of the blow-up criteria later on,

and

(3.21) G~1​(t):=∫ℝN∂tu⁡(x,t)​ψ1​(x,t)​𝑑x,G~2​(t):=∫ℝN∂tv⁡(x,t)​ψ2​(x,t)​𝑑x.\tilde{G}_{1}(t):=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\partial_{t}u(x,t)\psi_{1}(x,t)dx,\quad\tilde{G}_{2}(t):=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\partial_{t}v(x,t)\psi_{2}(x,t)dx.

The aim of the next two lemmas is to prove that the functions ε−1​Gi​(t){\varepsilon}^{-1}G_{i}(t) and ε−1​G~i​(t){\varepsilon}^{-1}\tilde{G}_{i}(t) are coercive. Indeed, as we will see later on in (3.22) and (3.35) below, we will improve the lower bounds already obtained for the functionals Fi​(t)F_{i}(t) and F~i​(t)\tilde{F}_{i}(t). This improvement will be useful in the proof of the main result of this article.

Although the techniques used here are somehow close to the ones in our previous work [6] (which studies the one single equation corresponding to (1.1)), but, the situation is slightly different for the system (1.1). (4.15) L2​(t)≥C3​ε8+C​∫T2t(T2+s)−(N−1)2​(q−1)+μ22−μ12​q​(L1​(s))q​𝑑s,∀t≥T2.L_{2}(t)\geq\frac{C_{3}{\varepsilon}}{8}+C\int_{T_{2}}^{t}(T_{2}+s)^{-\frac{(N-1)}{2}(q-1)+\frac{\mu_{2}}{2}-\frac{\mu_{1}}{2}q}(L_{1}(s))^{q}ds,\quad\forall\ t\geq T_{2}.

At this level, the remaining part of the proof is the same as the one in [18, Sections 4.2 and 4.3]. More precisely, here (4.14) (resp. (4.15) corresponds to (25) (resp. (26)) in [18]. Nevertheless, in the present work the shift of the dimension NN is with μi\mu_{i} instead of σ⁡(μi)\sigma(\mu_{i}) in [18], where σ⁡(μi)\sigma(\mu_{i}) is defined by (1.6).

This achieves the proof of Theorem 2.2.

5. Appendix

The aim of this appendix is to recall some properties of the function ρiη​(t)\rho_{i}^{\eta}(t), for i=1,2i=1,2, the solution of (3.3). Mainly, we will use the computations in [22]. Hence, we can write the expression of ρiη​(t)\rho_{i}^{\eta}(t) as follows:

(5.1) ρiη(t)=(η(t+1))μi+12Kδi2(η(t+1)),i=1,2,\rho^{\eta}_{i}(t)=(\eta(t+1))^{\frac{\mu_{i}+1}{2}}K_{\frac{\sqrt{\delta_{i}}}{2}}(\eta(t+1)),\ i=1,2,

where

Kν​(t)=∫0∞exp⁡(−t​cosh⁡ζ)​cosh⁡(ν​ζ)​𝑑ζ,ν∈ℝ.K_{\nu}(t)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\exp(-t\cosh\zeta)\cosh(\nu\zeta)d\zeta,\ \nu\in\mathbb{R}.

From the proof of [22, Lemma 2.1], one can see that

(5.2) 1ρiη​(t)d​ρiη​(t)d​t=μi+1+δi2​(t+1)−ηKδi2+1​(η​(t+1))Kδi2​(η​(t+1)),i=1,2.\frac{1}{\rho^{\eta}_{i}(t)}\frac{d\rho^{\eta}_{i}(t)}{dt}=\frac{\mu_{i}+1+\sqrt{\delta_{i}}}{2(t+1)}-\eta\frac{K_{\frac{\sqrt{\delta_{i}}}{2}+1}(\eta(t+1))}{K_{\frac{\sqrt{\delta_{i}}}{2}}(\eta(t+1))},\ i=1,2.

On the other hand, the function Kν​(t),ν∈ℝ,K_{\nu}(t),\nu\in{\mathbb{R}}, satisfies ([2])

(5.3) Kν(t)=π2​te−t(1+O(t−1),ast→∞.K_{\nu}(t)=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2t}}e^{-t}(1+O(t^{-1}),\quad\text{as}\ t\to\infty.

A combination of (5.2) and (5.3) yields

(5.4) 1ρiη​(t)d​ρiη​(t)d​t=−η+O(t−1),ast→∞,i=1,2.\frac{1}{\rho^{\eta}_{i}(t)}\frac{d\rho^{\eta}_{i}(t)}{dt}=-\eta+O(t^{-1}),\quad\text{as}\ t\to\infty,\ i=1,2.
